claim_verdicts.evidence: Middleware order (moniker >= aspnetcore-8.0): "The order that middleware appears in the app's `Program` file defines the order in which middleware are invoked on a request with the reverse order for the response." Same page: "Each middleware in the request pipeline is responsible for invoking the next middleware in the pipeline or short-circuiting the pipeline."

Intro list: each middleware "Can perform work before and after the next middleware in the pipeline." And: "Chain multiple request delegates together with Use. The `next` parameter represents the next delegate in the pipeline. You can typically perform actions both before and after the `next` delegate." The worked sample prints "can write to the response (1)", "(2)", "doesn't write (2)", "doesn't write (1)".

"Each middleware ... is responsible for invoking the next middleware in the pipeline or short-circuiting the pipeline. When a middleware short-circuits, it's called a terminal middleware because it prevents further middleware from processing the request." (:23) and "You can short-circuit the pipeline by *not* calling the *next* parameter." (:353). The hedge "usually after writing a response" is supported by :127 (static file middleware "processing a request for a static file and short-circuiting the rest of the pipeline").

Authentication concepts: "An authentication challenge is invoked by Authorization when an unauthenticated user requests an endpoint that requires authentication ... A JWT bearer scheme returning a 401 result with a `www-authenticate: bearer` header"; forbid "is called by Authorization when an authenticated user attempts to access a resource they're not permitted to access" -> "A JWT bearer scheme returning a 403 result". Live run of the stage-1 lab: POST /api/v1/orders with no token -> "HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized", "Www-Authenticate: Bearer".

`git -C examples/don-hang show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Program.cs`, lines 64-74: comment, UseMiddleware<ExceptionHandlingMiddleware>(), UseMiddleware<RequestLoggingMiddleware>(), UseCors(), UseAuthentication(), UseAuthorization(), MapControllers(), blank, Run(). The "own calls only" qualifier is right: WebApplication automatically adds UseDeveloperExceptionPage "first when the HostingEnvironment is Development" (the lab sets ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development) and UseRouting "second"; "User configured middleware and endpoints are added between UseRouting and UseEndpoints."

`git -C examples/don-hang show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Middleware/RequestLoggingMiddleware.cs` lines 9-24 match the lesson's block character for character: Stopwatch.StartNew(); await next(context); stopwatch.Stop(); logger.LogInformation("{Method} {Path} responded {StatusCode} in {ElapsedMs}ms", context.Request.Method, context.Request.Path, context.Response.StatusCode, stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds).

Live run: `docker compose up -d db api lab web` at stage-1 (clean tree, HEAD = stage-1 commit), then `curl -i -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/orders` -> "HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized ... Server: Kestrel ... Www-Authenticate: Bearer". `docker compose logs api` -> "info: DonHang.Api.Middleware.RequestLoggingMiddleware[0]" / "      POST /api/v1/orders responded 401 in 59ms". Containers removed afterwards.

Routing: "WebApplicationBuilder configures a middleware pipeline that wraps middleware added in Program.cs with UseRouting and UseEndpoints. However, apps can change the order in which UseRouting and UseEndpoints run by calling these methods explicitly"; "Endpoints execute at the position of UseEndpoints"; auth middleware "are placed between UseRouting and UseEndpoints so that they can: See which endpoint was selected by UseRouting." middleware8.md: UseRouting "is added second, if the user code didn't already call UseRouting". True of Đơn Hàng, not unconditional as written.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Unless the app calls `UseRouting` itself, ASP.NET Core wraps the middleware added in `Program.cs` with route matching at the start and endpoint execution at the end, so a request is matched to its endpoint before any middleware the app registered runs, and the matched endpoint is invoked only after every middleware has run without short-circuiting.

issues.quote: Moving `UseAuthorization` above `RequestLoggingMiddleware` would not just reorder two lines: a rejected request would then short-circuit before `RequestLoggingMiddleware` ever called `next`, so it would stop appearing in the log at all
issues.text: Unlisted claim: this counterfactual is nowhere in the claims ledger, and it hides a condition. Moving UseAuthorization above RequestLoggingMiddleware also moves it above UseCors and UseAuthentication, which the docs forbid: "CORS middleware, authentication middleware, and authorization middleware must appear in the order shown" and "UseCors must be placed after UseRouting and before UseAuthorization". The lesson presents the lost log line as the whole cost of a reorder that is documented-illegal for other reasons too.
issues.fix: Use the equivalent counterfactual that crosses nothing else: "moving `app.UseMiddleware<RequestLoggingMiddleware>()` below `app.UseAuthorization()` would make rejected requests stop appearing in the log". Add that as a claim in .meta.json (behavior, aspnetcore). Keep quiz q6's scenario in sync with whichever direction the prose uses; if the UseAuthorization-moves-up version is kept, add "(the docs also require UseAuthorization to stay after UseCors and UseAuthentication)".

issues.quote: the proposal moves `UseAuthorization` earlier, not `UseAuthentication` later, so that specific problem does not arise here
issues.text: False. The scenario moves UseAuthorization ahead of "the other wiring calls", which includes `app.UseAuthentication()`; relative order is all that matters, so UseAuthentication would indeed run after UseAuthorization — the docs' required order (CORS, authentication, authorization) would be broken. Option c is wrong only because nothing throws an exception, not because the ordering problem "does not arise". Key ('a') stays correct; the explanation teaches something untrue.
issues.fix: Rewrite c's explanation (en+vi): "Running `UseAuthentication` after `UseAuthorization` is exactly what this proposal would cause, and the docs require the opposite order — but nothing throws; the checkable cost the question asks about is the missing log line."

issues.quote: This would matter when the proposal also moved `app.MapControllers()` itself
issues.text: Repeats the mental-model error: where `app.MapControllers()` sits in the file does not decide when the endpoint runs. MapControllers only registers endpoints; "Endpoints execute at the position of UseEndpoints", which WebApplication adds at the end of the pipeline. Moving that line would not make endpoints "stop working". The vi text is also stronger than the en: "request được phép vẫn qua mọi bước kiểm tra và tới `app.MapControllers()`" describes the request as travelling to a wiring call.
issues.fix: Rewrite b's explanation (en+vi): "`app.MapControllers()` only registers endpoints; the endpoints it registers execute at the end of the pipeline wherever that line sits, so an authorized request still reaches `OrdersController.Create()` exactly as before." Align vi with en ("tới endpoint", not "tới app.MapControllers()").

issues.quote: and `MapControllers()` last, since it is the terminal step an authorized request finally reaches
issues.text: The question asks for registration order in the file, but the explanation justifies the last position by pipeline position — the same wrong model. `app.MapControllers()` is not a pipeline step: it registers endpoints, and "Endpoints execute at the position of UseEndpoints" (added at the end of the pipeline by WebApplication) regardless of where the line appears. Answer order b,d,a,c matches Program.cs lines 65-69 and stays correct.
issues.fix: Rewrite the explanation's tail (en+vi): "...and `MapControllers()` last in the file — it registers endpoints rather than adding a pipeline step, and those endpoints run at the end of the pipeline wherever this line sits."

issues.quote: Whatever was registered after the short-circuiting middleware — here, the endpoint `OrdersController.Create()` that routing had already matched — never runs at all.
issues.text: Calls the endpoint something "registered after the short-circuiting middleware". That is textually true only by accident here (MapControllers happens to be written after UseAuthorization) and is not the reason the endpoint does not run: endpoints execute at the end of the pipeline, at UseEndpoints, whatever the registration order.
issues.fix: "Everything further down the pipeline — including the endpoint, which runs only at the very end — never runs at all."

issues.quote: `UseAuthorization` comes last among them, right before `app.MapControllers()`, because it is the last thing allowed to say no before an allowed request's endpoint runs
issues.text: "right before `app.MapControllers()`" invites the reader back into the position-of-MapControllers model. What makes UseAuthorization the last check is that it is the last middleware registered, not the neighbouring line.
issues.fix: Drop the clause: "`UseAuthorization` comes last among them, because it is the last middleware allowed to say no before an allowed request's endpoint runs; where `app.MapControllers()` sits in the file doesn't change that."

issues.quote: exactly the change Try it below checks for
issues.text: Try it applies no change: it runs one curl against the order as it stands and reads the log. It demonstrates that the log line exists today, not what would happen after the reorder.
issues.fix: "— the opposite of what Try it below shows with the order as it stands."

issues.quote: E -->|No| F[401 or 403, written here]
issues.text: "written here" conflicts with the prose and with claim 4: the status is produced by the authentication scheme UseAuthorization challenges (JWT bearer returns 401 with `www-authenticate: bearer`), not written by the authorization middleware itself.
issues.fix: Relabel the node: `F[Request stops: 401 or 403 written on its behalf]`.

issues.quote: M[Routing matches the endpoint] --> A[ExceptionHandlingMiddleware]
issues.text: "routing" is used three times (diagram node; "the endpoint routing already matched"; "that routing had already matched") but is neither in this lesson's `vocab` nor in known_vocab before it, and is never glossed — the reader is told a step exists, before the lesson's own first middleware, with no idea what it is. It is also outside `depth_notes`, which only authorises the UseAuthorization/[Authorize] observation.
issues.fix: Gloss it once on first use, e.g. "routing — the built-in step that decides which endpoint a URL belongs to — has already matched the endpoint before any of Đơn Hàng's middleware runs", and either add `routing` to this lesson's `vocab` in track.yaml or extend `depth_notes` to permit naming it (as was done for UseAuthorization).

issues.quote: so it is still on its way back out when the short-circuit happens further down — which is why it still gets a chance to log the outcome
issues.text: Sequence is inverted: when the short-circuit happens, RequestLoggingMiddleware has finished its way-in work and is awaiting `next`; its way-out half starts only after the short-circuit returns.
issues.fix: "so it is still waiting for `next` to return when the short-circuit happens further down — and that return is what lets its after-`next` half run and log the outcome."

issues.quote: the line that must run before the method can read `context.Response.StatusCode`
issues.text: `context.Response.StatusCode` is readable at any point (it is 200 by default); `await next(context)` is what makes the value the one the request actually got. As written the stem states something false about HttpResponse, though the answer "next" is unambiguous.
issues.fix: Restate the stem: "the line that must run before `context.Response.StatusCode` holds the status this request actually got is `await ___(context);`".

beyond_scope: Route matching as a pipeline step that runs before the app's own middleware (diagram node "Routing matches the endpoint" plus two mentions of what routing "had already matched") — factually required to avoid the earlier wrong model, but outside the outline and depth_notes, and the term is never explained.

issues.quote: **middleware** — one step in the pipeline a request passes through
issues.text: "pipeline" is the word the whole lesson leans on and the first thing I meet, but it is never bolded or defined. The closest I get is the third bullet, "pipeline order — the order the `app.Use...` calls appear in Program.cs", which explains the order, not what the pipeline is. I know `pipe` from the shell (`a | b`), so I half-guess a chain, but I am guessing.
issues.fix: In the first Core concepts bullet, make the pipeline explicit on first use: "**middleware** — one step in the chain of steps (the pipeline) every request passes through before it reaches an endpoint, in the order its `app.Use...` call was registered; …".

issues.quote: B[RequestLoggingMiddleware, UseCors, UseAuthentication]
issues.text: `UseCors` appears in the diagram and in the `Program.cs` block, and no sentence anywhere mentions it. I cannot tell what it does, whether it can stop my request like `UseAuthorization` does, or why it sits where it sits — so when I check the code against the diagram I have one line I cannot account for.
issues.fix: Add one clause in section 5 after "…so it logs every request regardless of what happens later": "; `app.UseCors()` and `app.UseAuthentication()` are steps ASP.NET Core supplies, and this lesson only needs the fact that they run between those two and `UseAuthorization`".

issues.quote:
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
issues.text: Two calls whose names differ by a few letters; only the second is ever explained. Section 6 and the summary then use "unauthenticated" and "unauthorized" for what looks like the same situation, so I cannot tell whether they mean one thing or two, nor which of the two calls reacts to my missing `Authorization` header.
issues.fix: Add one sentence in section 5 after "…because it is the last thing allowed to say no before an allowed request's endpoint runs": "`UseAuthentication` works out who is asking from the request's `Authorization` header; `UseAuthorization` then decides whether that caller may run this endpoint."

issues.quote: for an endpoint marked `[Authorize]`, it stops the request instead of calling the next step when not allowed
issues.text: `[Authorize]` shows up once, in passing, and appears in no code block in the lesson. I do not know what "marked" means here, where the mark is written, or how I would check whether `OrdersController.Create()` has one. That matters because this mark is what decides whether `UseAuthorization` stops my request at all — the second half of the question section 2 asked me.
issues.fix: Extend that sentence: "…for an endpoint whose method carries the `[Authorize]` attribute — `OrdersController.Create()` does — it stops the request instead of calling the next step when not allowed; endpoints without that attribute pass straight through."

issues.quote: You send `POST /api/v1/orders` with no `Authorization` header and get back `401` almost at once.
issues.text: Section 2 ends by asking "what decides whether a request gets stopped there at all?". The answer I am given is "when not allowed", and nothing ever says why sending no `Authorization` header makes me not allowed. So I finish the lesson able to say which call stopped me, but not able to answer the second question it asked me.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after "…and a `401` (or `403`) is written on its behalf.": "The request in the situation is not allowed because it carried no `Authorization` header, so no caller was identified for `UseAuthorization` to approve."

issues.quote: Before any of Đơn Hàng's own middleware runs, routing already works out which endpoint a request's path and method match
issues.text: I go to `Program.cs` to find this first step and there is no line for it — every line in the block is an `app.Use...` or `MapControllers`. So I cannot tell who runs routing or where it is configured. "Đơn Hàng's own middleware" also implies there are other middleware that are not ours, and I am never told which of the six lines are which.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after that clause: "That matching step is not one of the lines in `Program.cs` below — ASP.NET Core puts it in front of them for you; "Đơn Hàng's own" means the two `app.UseMiddleware<...>` classes written in this repo."

issues.quote: E -->|Yes| G[The matched endpoint runs: OrdersController.Create]
issues.text: Every arrow points one way and the picture ends at G (or at F). But the lesson's main payoff — a step acting again "on the way out", which is why the `401` still gets logged — has no arrow at all. When I try to narrate the Try it result from the diagram, the part I most need is missing, and node F looks like a dead end from which nothing can come back.
issues.fix: Add a return path to the diagram, e.g. `G --> R[Response travels back out]` and `F --> R`, then `R --> B2[... after `next` returns: RequestLoggingMiddleware logs]`, keeping the labels to names already used in the prose.

issues.quote: // the terminal middleware (auth, routing) that decides how to answer it.
issues.text: The comment in the code puts routing last and calls auth "terminal"; the diagram puts routing first, and the prose says the endpoint is the terminal thing. Reading both on one screen I cannot tell which order is true, and "terminal" seems to mean two different things.
issues.fix: Add one sentence right after the block: "The comment's "routing" means `app.MapControllers()` at the end of the list — the matching itself already happened before any of these lines, as the diagram shows."

issues.quote: public sealed class RequestLoggingMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, ILogger<RequestLoggingMiddleware> logger)
issues.text: I cannot connect `app.UseMiddleware<RequestLoggingMiddleware>()` to this class. Nothing says who calls `InvokeAsync`, how often, or that the `next` the prose keeps talking about is this `RequestDelegate` constructor parameter. The class implements no interface I could follow, so from the text alone this code just sits there.
issues.fix: Add one sentence before the block: "`app.UseMiddleware<RequestLoggingMiddleware>()` hands this class the next step as its `next` parameter and calls its `InvokeAsync` once per request."

issues.quote: `context.Response.StatusCode` is read only in that second half
issues.text: `HttpContext context` is new to me. The prose talks about `context.Request.Method` and `context.Response.StatusCode` as if I knew what `context` is and why the request and the response both hang off the same object — which is exactly the point being made about reading the status after `next`.
issues.fix: Add one clause on first mention: "`context` is the object ASP.NET Core passes through every step, carrying both the incoming request and the response being built — which is why `context.Response.StatusCode` is read only in that second half, …".

issues.quote: uses just the top half of that shape; a step that also touches the response after `next` returns uses the bottom half too
issues.text: I re-read this twice. "That shape" has no picture — the diagram has no halves — so "top half" and "bottom half" are a metaphor I have to build myself while learning the idea they describe.
issues.fix: Replace with plain words: "…uses only its before-`next` part; a step that also touches the response after `next` returns uses its after-`next` part as well."

issues.quote: var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
issues.text: Four names in the block (`Stopwatch`, `ILogger<T>`, `LogInformation`, the `{Method} {Path}` placeholders) are never mentioned, so I spend time deciding whether they matter before realising only `await next(context)` and the lines after it are the point.
issues.fix: Add one clause before the block: "the stopwatch and logger lines are only there to produce the log line; the two things to look at are `await next(context)` and what sits after it".

issues.quote: a `401` (or `403`) is written on its behalf
issues.text: I do not know when a request gets `401` and when `403`, nor who the "its" is that something else writes on behalf of. It is a small thing, but it is the exact status my Try it is supposed to check.
issues.fix: Replace with: "a `401` is written for a request that identified no caller at all (the case in the situation); a `403` when a caller is known but not permitted".

issues.quote: With the lab running (`scripts/up.sh`), run `curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/orders`
issues.text: "the lab", `scripts/up.sh`, `curl -i` and `docker compose logs api` are all new names. I can copy-paste them, so I am not stuck, but I do not know what I started or where step 2's output comes from.

issues.text: In q1, q2, q5 and q6 the correct option repeats a sentence of the lesson almost word for word (q2's key is the Suggested answer; q5's is the second "Beginners often think" correction). issues.quote: False, because `RequestLoggingMiddleware` already called `next` and is waiting for it to return; a short-circuit further down still counts as `next` returning, just earlier.
issues.text: Option c is roughly three times longer than a, b and d and is the only one with a two-clause explanation. On a true/false question with two "False" options I would pick the elaborate one on shape alone.
issues.fix: Shorten c to one clause ("False — it already called `next`, and a short-circuit still makes `next` return") and give d a comparable length, so no option stands out.

issues.quote: This would be a real cost when running one middleware after another caused a framework error
issues.text: The wrong-option explanations in q6 all start with "This would matter when…" / "This would be true when…", describing a situation that is not happening. I read c's twice and still could not tell whether it was saying an error does happen or does not.
issues.fix: Start each wrong-option explanation in q6 with the plain fact instead: e.g. c -> "Nothing in ASP.NET Core throws because of this reordering; the real cost is the missing log line in option a."

skipped_steps: "Before any of Đơn Hàng's own middleware runs, routing already works out which endpoint a request's path and method match" — no line in the Program.cs block corresponds to this step, and "own" is never contrasted with anything.
"for an endpoint marked `[Authorize]`, it stops the request ... when not allowed" — what marks an endpoint, and what makes a request "not allowed", are never said.
